utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So -- but we have time enough if there should be any other additional exhibit to be necessary to be admitted into evidence, then we can do it later. Before we start with the formal proceedings, I think some clarifications are necessary. This Trial Chamber is seized only with the events in Glogova the 9th of May 1992. The development to this very day, starting on or about the 19th of December 1991, at a meeting convened in Sarajevo presided over by Radovan Karadzic, that is referred to in paragraph 10 of the factual basis, until and including the 11th of May when the meeting in Pale was held, once again Mr. Karadzic being present. I have to emphasise this for two reasons: The application of the principle of non bis in idem, that is, you, Mr. Deronjic, will not be prosecuted a second time is limited to the attack on Glogova only. That's explicitly stated in paragraph 11(d) of the plea agreement. You can still be indicted for all maybe following crimes you might have been involved in, including Srebrenica, before this Tribunal or in other countries having jurisdiction as well. You should not live under the wrong impression that having pleaded guilty in this Glogova case creates an obstacle for other prosecutions in relation to other events. As regards the prosecution and investigation before this Tribunal, this is a matter for the Prosecutor's policy only. Opposed to other legal systems, a Chamber of this Tribunal has not the power to order investigations or to order the Prosecution on concrete other events, even there might be reason to do so, with only two exceptions - this is Rule 91 - in the case of false testimony under solemn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. declaration and Rule 77, this is contempt of the Tribunal. Therefore, this hearing and the envisaged testimony of Mr. Deronjic is limited to the aforementioned period of time only. However, we have to discuss all relevant sentencing factors; gravity of crime, aggravating and mitigating factors. In this context, and I have to emphasise "in this context alone", I already in the plea hearing had asked the OTP whether there are any additional commitments by the Prosecution to Mr. Deronjic, especially whether there is or not any commitment not to indict Mr. Deronjic for a possible involvement in the Srebrenica massacre. On page 46 of the transcript of this hearing, it reads the answer given by Mr. Harmon: "Mr. President, Your Honours, all of the promises that have been made to Mr. Deronjic are set forth in the plea agreement. There are no other promises made to Mr. Deronjic, no other agreements made with Mr. Deronjic or his counsel. In respect of the events in 1995 in Srebrenica, notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Deronjic's name may have come up in the context of other trials, an indictment against Mr. Deronjic for those events is not warranted." May I ask the Prosecution, do you have to add anything to this answer? Has anything changed since the 30th of September in the light of the numerous testimonies given by Mr. Deronjic in other cases, and is there any commitment not to indict or the intention to indict Mr. Deronjic also on -- in relation to other events? This is limited, the question is limited, for the mere purpose that we can evaluate what we can take into account as mitigating factor and what not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my answer has not changed in respect of whether or not there is -- Mr. Deronjic will be indicted for Srebrenica. I said then and I will say again today, and if Your Honours wish a more comprehensive explanation, I am prepared to give it to you. Do you want me to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, since July of 1995, my office has investigated continuously the events in Srebrenica. I personally was a legal officer who was assigned to that investigation in July of 1995. I have reviewed the evidence in the Srebrenica case extensively. As Your Honours know or may know, I was the lawyer for the Office of the Prosecutor that drafted and returned the indictment against Mr. Karadzic in the beginning of this Tribunal; the indictment against Mr. -- General Mladic; the indictment against Drazen Erdemovic; and I was the chief Prosecutor in the case of Radoslav Krstic. I would say that next to Mr. McCloskey in my office, I know the evidence in the Srebrenica case very well. I have reviewed that evidence. I know that evidence is not available to Your Honours. But I have reviewed it, and I have consulted with Mr. McCloskey about that particular event, consulted with him on numerous occasions. The Prosecutor in the course of discharging her independent judgement in her function as the Prosecutor has returned 13 indictments, public indictments, against individuals who were responsible for the killing operation in Srebrenica. The killing operation in Srebrenica was a military-run operation, and the people against whom indictments have been returned have been, and I will name them: Ratko Mladic, who was the chief of the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff; Radovan Karadzic, who was the supreme commander; General Krstic, who was the Drina Corps commander, he was prosecuted and convicted and received the sentence of 46 years for his involvement in the case; Momir Nikolic, who was the Drina Corps security chief, he pled guilty, received a sentence of 27 years; Dragan Obrenovic, who was the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, he pled guilty before this Tribunal and received a sentence of 17 years; Drazen Erdemovic, who was a member of the 10th Sabotage Battalion and who participated in a mass execution at the Branjevo Military Farm pled guilty, he was sentenced on his second plea agreement to five years; Vinko Pandurevic, who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, was indicted, he is a fugitive from justice; Drago Nikolic who was the Zvornik security chief has been indicted, he is a fugitive from justice; Colonel Ljubisa Beara, who was the VRS Main Staff chief of security, was indicted, he is a fugitive from justice; Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, who was the Drina Corps assistant commander for security, has been indicted and was and is a fugitive from justice; Ljubomir Borovcanin, deputy commander of the special police brigade for the RS Ministry of the Interior, was indicted for his involvement in these events, he also is a fugitive; Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, the Bratunac Brigade commander, and Dragan Jokic, the chief of the engineers from the Zvornik Brigade both are currently in trial in this institution. Now, I will tell Your Honours that after having consulted with Mr. McCloskey, after having consulted with members of the team, my answer insofar as our intentions and our assessment of the evidence in respect of Mr. Deronjic's involvement has not changed and it has not changed in light of the testimony, the many testimonies that he has given to this Tribunal. I hope that answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For this part, no doubt it's a comprehensive answer, and it shows all the efforts of the Prosecution invested in the attempt to get all these persons -- to bring all these persons to justice. But I have to come back to the second part of the question, and that is whether or not there is any other additional commitment to Mr. Deronjic and any other promise given to him. I refer to Rule 62 ter (C) where it reads that if a plea agreement has been reached by the parties, the Trial Chamber shall require the disclosure of the agreement in open session or, on showing of good cause, in closed session. Indeed, this happened. We received a plea agreement. The only question, the only open question, is is it indeed the full plea agreement, or was something omitted? We admitted into -- in public into evidence the understanding of the parties. And I quote the Prosecution in case Prosecutor versus Blagojevic: "The understanding of the parties should normally be something you have as a part of the plea agreement." So we were taken by surprise when reading the submitted documents that indeed there was such an understanding of the parties. And the question for us is, one, a technical; and second, one that goes to the merits. Do you regard this understanding as forming part of the plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I will explain why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- if Your Honour wishes. The plea agreement that has been presented and presented in open court sets forth all of the understandings and promises that were made by the Prosecutor, and those are set forth in paragraph 11(a) through (f). Those promises, and no other promises, were made to Mr. Deronjic to induce him to enter a plea. The understanding of the parties, however, is a different document and formed no part of the plea agreement. The understanding of the parties was an understanding at a time when Mr. Deronjic was reluctant to provide a full statement to the Office of the Prosecutor unless he had an understanding that was written, and we set that forth with my colleagues from the Defence. And they will confirm this. This document, understanding, was in order to induce Mr. Deronjic to feel free to talk to us without fear that those statements would be used against him in a later prosecution. This understanding of the parties was executed every day when we interviewed -- when I interviewed and the investigator interviewed Mr. Deronjic. It was not used in any way to induce him to plead guilty, and I will take responsibility for paragraph 16, because paragraph 16 is not as clearly drafted as it should have been and may well have misled this Court. But I will assert to Your Honours and my colleagues, I will confirm this to Your Honours, this understanding of the parties was not part of the plea agreement. It had no part of the -- it was not part of the plea agreement whatsoever. And I will defer, if Your Honours wish, to my Defence colleagues who can confirm that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the only remaining question is whether one can assess paragraph 7 of the understanding of the parties that the Prosecutor agrees that anything said by Mr. Deronjic during the interview will not be used as evidence in legal proceedings against him before the Tribunal. Isn't this a promise given to Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you referring, Your Honour, to paragraph 10 of the understanding of the parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That was a promise that was made to Mr. Deronjic in order to ensure that he would talk to us. Absent a promise like that, he would not talk to us and we would not have had the benefit of Mr. Deronjic's assistance in many cases. So this was a promise that was made as part of an understanding to give him the confidence to talk to us at a time when he had no legal obligation to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. This understanding of the parties is signed, was signed by you, and it's in the responsibility, and of course, in the jurisdiction of the Prosecution alone, it's a question of the policy of the Prosecution. And therefore, if you state that does not form part of the plea agreement, then the Trial Chamber understands that this Chamber is not seized at all with this understanding of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence would like to confirm literally everything what our learned colleague from the OTP has said. And it, in fact, was not and we never considered this to be a part of the plea agreement. And therefore, we are -- the Defence is completely in agreement with what Mr. Mark Harmon has said. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank both parties for this clarification. The Defence has indicated to the Chamber that they want to call Mr. Deronjic as a witness in his own case. Is it still the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may Mr. Deronjic please be escorted to the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Deronjic, acting now not as an accused in this case but as a witness to give a solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. I have reasons to inform you and to admonish you that, in fact, you have to tell us the truth and nothing but the truth. The reason why I emphasise this can be found on page 6407 of the hearing in the case Prosecutor versus Mr. Blagojevic, Thursday 22nd January 2004. There, you stated: "I said that my earlier statements were incorrect because there are several reasons, one of them I did mention. That was fear for my own safety or maybe my wrong thinking about wrong political implications if this truth were to come out. And ultimately, I wanted to use my right, which is well known, that I'm not obliged to tell the truth if it can harm me in any way at that point. So I did not give an entirely truthful statement for those reasons. But I do not agree that those statements are completely untrue. They are partially untrue..." And then it continues with a remark to Mr. Karnavas. Maybe you are under the wrong impression based on the judicial system you're living in because in your system, like most other civil-law systems, an accused, of course, doesn't enjoy the right not to tell the truth but he can't be held criminally responsible for testimony under solemn declaration which is false. This is not true in principle in common-law system, especially not under the Rules of this Tribunal. Under Rule 91, it is provided that false testimony under solemn declaration is punishable and is punishable with a fine up to 100.000 euros or a term of imprisonment of seven years, or both. And the Chamber may instruct the Prosecutor to start necessary investigations. So therefore, it should be absolutely clear for you that you have the possibility to remain silent in toto, that means that you don't give any statement at all, or that you remain silent in relation to certain questions. However, you have not the right, as you said in this previous testimony, not to tell the truth if it can harm you in any way at that point. So in case, in balancing, you come to the conclusion it is in your interest and you don't want to give us an answer, then please remain silent but don't give us a wrong answer. Did you understand this admonition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time enough that we can start with your testimony. Of course, you are the witness for the Defence, and you can and may be guided by the Defence. However, as I indicated already earlier, it should be limited and it has to be limited to the case before us, that is the attack on Glogova, and the events from 19 December 1991 until 12 May 1992. Hopefully, with all details and also in order to clarify the one or other discrepancy the Chamber identified when trying to marry the indictment with the factual basis. The Chamber has given a list of maybe discrepancies or overlaps of your statements. And I think in preparation of this hearing, you have discussed this with your counsel. But it might be helpful that you start telling us in context what has happened since this very 19th of December 1991, who invited for this meeting, who was presiding over, who was present, and in particular what were the issues that were discussed this very day until the events in Glogova. I think it's preferable that you tell us in context in your own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Agius is excused for two minutes if the parties do not object. And we proceed for these two minutes formally under Rule 15. Yes. Maybe in order that also Judge Agius can follow your testimony, especially the start of your testimony, we should wait until he comes back. Therefore, let's wait a second, and we may use this time. Are there any additional comments to be made by one of the parties in relation to the scheduling of this case, anything not yet foreseen in the scheduling order?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would just like to bring to the attention of Your Honours that I am due to start a trial on the 3rd of February in the Krajisnik case, and I received a phone call last night asking me if I could attend a 65 ter conference at 5.00 on Wednesday night. I said I was unavailable because I was here. I informed the legal officer that there was an optional day on the following day, Thursday, and I asked him to ask Judge Orie if the 65 ter conference could be scheduled on the Thursday. I would very much like to attend that 65 ter conference given that I will be starting a very important trial within a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I take it that you will be present tomorrow here, and Judge Orie has decided to postpone the 65 ter conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I left that as a work in progress, Your Honour. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be here tomorrow for sure, and when I heard you mention possibly we might go a third day, it caused me some alarm, so I am hopeful, too, that we will finish in two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We share your hope. We waited until you come back. Mr. Deronjic, you may start your testimony, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had intended to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. start from April 1991 in order to show a connection with these events. However, if Your Honours deem this unnecessary, I will skip it over. If you agree, however, I would like to say a few sentences about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is your testimony. Therefore, we don't want to limit your testimony if there is a link. So please, proceed as you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my last interview that I gave to the OTP in October last year, I touched upon a series of events from 1991, and this was in connection with April 1991. This seems to me to be the month - I am not, unfortunately, sure of the precise date of that session, but I did say it was in April 1991 - this seems to be an event that heralded a change in the political climate and an abandoning of the platform of the Serbian Democratic Party which had up until that point been public. In the political sense, this could be described as an effort to preserve Yugoslavia as it had existed up to then. I explained some details that occurred during that meeting, and I have nothing special to add. The meeting was held in Sarajevo, and unfortunately to this day I'm unable to remember whether it was in the Holiday Inn or perhaps in another location, because during 1991 I attended very few meetings in Sarajevo, and I remember we held all of these meetings in one of two places, the Holiday Inn and the Srbijanka Villa in Ilidza, a suburb of Sarajevo. My conclusion today is that this event and this meeting took place in Holiday Inn, but I cannot be a hundred per cent certain about this. At this meeting which was of a plenary nature, that is, the main board extended with all the presidents of the SDS municipal boards and the deputies in the assembly, the joint assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina - of course, I'm referring to the Serb deputies - the top leadership of the SDS, including President Karadzic who at that time was only the president of the SDS. The topic of the meeting was something that was usually referred to as the political security situation at any given moment. In the context of the events which are well known and the general political circumstances in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, of course, this had to do with certain decisions by the Presidency of the SFRY, and certain decisions made by the leadership of Serbia. I have mentioned some of these that stick in my memory as very interesting events. And as I said, just before this meeting, a political event had taken place in Croatia; that is, the decision of the government of the previously formed Serbian Autonomous Region of the Krajina on joining the Krajina to the Republic of Serbia. This was the declaratory act of secession of the Serbian people in Croatia and their annexation to the Republic of Serbia. As far as I know, at a subsequent session of the Assembly of Serbia, this secession proposal was rejected. I'm not aware of the reasons, but I do know that this event drew a lot of attention among the members of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina and influenced their actions. The political decisions made by the politicians in the Serbian Krajina and in Croatia caused us to convene this meeting, or rather the party leadership to convene it. I apologise to the interpreters. I will try to slow down. The meeting was public. I think that the media also broadcast part of that meeting. It was held in central Sarajevo. As far as I recall, just President Karadzic addressed the meeting, and he explained the complex political conditions in which our activities were taking place at that point in time. I am talking about this meeting for a different reason. For the first time at this meeting, I heard in Mr. Karadzic's speech some terms and formulations or assertions which were not familiar to me and were not contained in the programme documents of the Serbian Democratic Party. He stated a sentence I remembered on that occasion, and I remembered it because I, myself, and a series of other local politicians quoted that sentence also in some of our addresses. And that's how I remembered it. Mr. Karadzic said, I'm not quoting, I'm just conveying the sense of his sentence, If there is no longer a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbs only have one option left, and that is Greater Serbia. That is the essence of that sentence. I'm not quite sure after 12 years that I can quote every single word, but that is the gist of it. And I heard that expression, "Greater Serbia," for the first time then, because until then I didn't hear it formally or informally, and I hadn't heard it as being contained in any of the programme documents of the SDS. Of course, he also talked about the political climate in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, and his address focussed on one event which I remembered, and I think the majority of the participants at the time remembered it. And that is that the SDA submitted in the joint, the common assembly, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a declaration on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its secession from Yugoslavia. All those speeches and events and those at that meeting had to do with that document which we interpreted at the time as an unconstitutional attempt to -- for the breakaway of Bosnia and Herzegovina from our common state. After that official large meeting in which numerous participants took part and which was chaired by President Karadzic, I had the lucky chance of finding myself near him in a smaller company. To this day, with a high degree of probability, I can say that this conversation took place at the National Restaurant in Sarajevo in smaller company. I recall some details regarding that meeting. I remember that we opened and drank a bottle of wine. I remember that. That we were there briefly. When I say "briefly," I mean about an hour. Besides myself, Mr. Zekic was also in the company with whom I actually came into that group in the first place; I knew him at the time. Then Mr. Ostojic, whom I knew from before because he came to the founding ceremony of the SDS in Bratunac in 1991. There was Mrs. Slobodanka Hrvacanin. Probably there were some other participants. I do not want to make a mistake, but I'm sure about these people. There were some three or four people there. I didn't know all of them at the time. And except for Karadzic and Ostojic, I don't think any of them knew me. Our conversation touched upon similar topics in the restaurant, and at one point Karadzic also touched upon these topics, and he said that it was agreed that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be divided up. That was the first time that I heard of it. And this made me pay attention. Since I didn't have the opportunity and I wasn't very well known in the political circles, I didn't dare to ask any questions about that, but I did listen carefully. Ms. Slobodanka Hrvacanin joined the conversation. She was considered in the fate of the Serbs in Zenica. I recall a few sentences exchanged between her and Karadzic on this topic, whether the Serbs of Zenica or Zenica itself was part of this decision, and on what side it would find itself. That was the essence of what they talked about. But I couldn't clearly see what the plan was regarding this division. However, at the time Mr. Karadzic used one sentence. He said one thing which I remembered, and it seemed to be a kind of suggestion to us who were there. He said: "If anyone was afraid to participate in this, then they should not take part in that. I will understand if people fear this. It's natural if somebody does not wish to take part. It's normal that they should say so." Of course, this did not refer only to us. And so none of those present responded to this question. Why am I talking about this meeting? It seems to me that -- I'm afraid that I'm repeating myself perhaps, but a kind of initiative was voiced there relating to events which followed in Bosnia and Herzegovina and related to something that was not contained in any of the documents in -- relating to the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it was not contained in any of the programmes of the SDS. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I commented to a certain degree what happened with Mr. Zekic on our way back. I commented on what happened at the meeting because he was more a part of all of that. But I really did get the impression that he was not at all or quite well informed about the change of some strategic programme, principles of the Serbian Democratic Party. In that context, I don't have much new information to this very day, and I wasn't able to refresh my recollection about these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting you that we come to one point and that we don't forget it. If you already touched upon the events in April 1991, in your testimony you make reference to, on page 4 and paragraph 8 and 9, it reads: "Karadzic boasted having personally convinced Milosevic that Serbs are to arm themselves, meaning that they had no confidence in the JNA. They did not believe that the JNA could protect Serbs. Karadzic wanted to arm the people. Djukic has told us that we need to arm ourselves, and that at the SDS level it had been determined what people ought to be involved in this and in which regions. At that time, he said that Goran Zekic and I were tasked with Srebrenica, Bratunac, and that area." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's correct. But it's not the same meeting. I apologise. This meeting relates to my meeting with Mr. Djukic. It also took place in April 1991, but this meeting was held in Milici, and this is a meeting that I wanted to mention right after I finish with this meeting that I'm talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Now, I would like to talk about events which followed this meeting in Sarajevo, which I was talking about. And I will try to remember everything that is important. In the month of April, certain talk about the arming of the Serbs began. When I say "talks," I primarily mean my conversations with Goran Zekic who was the only person from the region of Birac who had some kind of high post in the SDS and the state. He was a deputy in the assembly. He was a member of the main board. And he also had some duties, professional duties, in the assembly itself so that he was often in Sarajevo. He met the political leadership of the SDS, and he did have certain information. His information was better than that of us who were not really included in those circles. So in some conversations, and I mention the details where these conversations took place I don't want to repeat myself, he said he was working on the arming of the Serbs and he was doing in in an illegal way through smugglers and these methods. In April, in late April, probably in late April, I had the opportunity to attend a meeting in Milici, and I explained what happened at this meeting. So this is that meeting, Your Honour, that you mentioned. This is a meeting with Mr. Djukic. It was held in Milici in the fish restaurant, the only or the best-known restaurant in that little town. Just to explain briefly, even though I've explained that before, Mr. Djukic, Rajko Djukic, that's who I am thinking of, is a very well-known political and commercial figure in that area. He is a director of many years' standing, and to this day he was a director of the bauxite mines. He was a person who in the earlier political system was a businessman and a politician who had a -- who played a major role. He is believed to be one of the founders of the SDS and one of the first financiers of the SDS. So he's a person who is connected to the political leadership, the republican leadership of the SDS. And in the beginning, I don't know for how long, he was the president of the Executive Board of the SDS. He was a man who knew the situation in the political leadership of the SDS very well. And now I'm talking about something that I heard indirectly. He was believed to be very highly rated in Serbia in the political circles of the SPS, and JUL, a party which was founded later. So his name was also connected to that party as well. So his authority in that region was definite. I don't want to give you any more details about how this meeting was convened. But at this meeting, he said that the SDS political leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina decided that Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina should arm themselves. That is when he said that Karadzic personally convinced Mr. Milosevic, the President of Serbia at the time, to arm the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know the broader context, but Karadzic was probably just interested in the Serbs in Bosnia. I had the opportunity at a subsequent meeting, one of the subsequent meetings with Mr. Karadzic, it's very difficult for me to remember exactly when this meeting took place. I don't think it was any formal meeting. It was just an encounter. And I literally heard the sentence from Mr. Karadzic. He confirmed to me, or not to me, but he did address somebody who was present. He said that he was the one who made it possible for Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina to arm themselves via Milosevic, and he said that the reasons why he made such a request was his disagreement in the role of the military in the resolution of the political crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Yugoslavia as well. He was thinking of certain political disagreements about how the army, as a multiethnic unit as it was in the former Yugoslavia, would adapt to certain requirements and changes which were taking place from day to day. That is what he probably thought of. That's how he explained it. So there were certain disagreements at the time as regards the army between the different leaderships. Mr. Milosevic's position on the JNA was that he had full confidence in the JNA in the way it was formulated during the previous period. What was our position, Goran Zekic's and my position on this? I've already described it; I don't want to repeat all the information, how Djukic gave him the paper with the name and address of the man we were supposed to contact. I will skip over those details. So in early May, Goran Zekic and myself went to Belgrade. He collected me in the morning. We left for Belgrade. He said he had made the contact that had been agreed upon. We arrived there. I described in detail who this man was. I recall every particular detail of that meeting. A large number of details. Mr. Milosevic in his case tried to dispute this somewhat, but there is no doubt that I was there, that I saw it, and that I heard what I said I heard. I don't want to repeat the details. So the agreement with Kertes, I talked about him, was reached in Belgrade. The way in which he came forward at the time was not something that appealed to me. I thought that he was very indiscreet on topics that one should not be indiscreet about. What was important, what I believe was very important, is Goran Zekic asked Mr. Kertes a question, and that is what Serbia intended to do in the political resolution of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was its role and intention towards the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina? When I heard that, Mr. Kertes said that the position or the decision or -- of the political and state leadership of Serbia was that 50 kilometres from the Drina, and we are precisely from that area, that all of that would be Serb. This is what he said. We didn't comment much about what he said. We accepted what he said in the way that we accepted it. We had the opportunity later to comment on that a little bit. At that meeting, the first arms delivery to Bratunac was agreed upon, and that was the only one in which I participated in directly. I described how this was carried out, and I don't think it's necessary to go into all of the details. They have been precisely described with the names of the participants, those who carried it out, how the weapons were transferred to Bratunac, to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to Bratunac and Srebrenica. When I spoke about weapons, I provided my detailed information about the weapons. I was no longer involved in that afterwards. The weapons came through the Yugoslav Army at the time. I mentioned the two centres from where the weapons came to Bratunac and Srebrenica, and they are Tuzla and Uzice. The Uzice Corps, I mentioned the persons who were on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. key posts at the time in those military units. I did not meet any of those people. I mentioned the persons who told myself and Goran Zekic that the weapons were being distributed through the military. I already described how in the summer of 1991, the Serbs in Bratunac and Srebrenica armed themselves. These were the activities of the Territorial Defence. I think I explained that very clearly. I explained what the concept or the idea of the TO was and how this was implemented on the ground. I don't think that there is anything that needs to be added to this because it is quite clear. I did mention an example, an unusual event that some party, Movement for Yugoslavia or new communism or something like that - I don't remember exactly what it's called - also sent an arms shipment to Bratunac. What is a relevant fact, which confirms that there was a strategy involved here which was being clearly implemented, is the fact that in the autumn or at the end of the summer 1991, a centre was formed in Milici from which further distribution of weapons was carried out. I don't know to this day the origin of the weapons in those warehouses in Milici, but I did go there once and agreed for a shipment for Bratunac. I went with Goran Zekic. I said that I saw Mr. Djukic there, and local police and some other local people from the neighbouring municipality. With regard to weapons, I think I have given sufficient relevant proof that all this was planned by the top leadership of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the military structures in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the state structures in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you very much for this detailed discussion. However, I think it need not be repeated everything we have already admitted into evidence. In conclusion, my final question would be that once again, is it true, Mr. Deronjic, that in April -- already in April, Mr. Djukic told you and Mr. Goran Zekic that you were tasked with Srebrenica, Bratunac, and that area? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we have to make -- we have to have a break in about four minutes. If you could briefly touch upon the events the 14th and 15th October 1991, and then after the break proceed with the events in December 1991 in order to come as soon as possible to the core events of this case; that's the attack on Glogova. If you could make use of the remaining minutes before the break to briefly touch upon the 14th and 15th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I shall, of course, very briefly mention these events. The event of the 15th October 1991 is well known, of course. The joint assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed a declaration on the establishing of a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was tabled by the deputies of the SDA. After this, the SDS deputies walked out of the assembly, and these are well-known events, and I have no new information in connection with this. What is relevant for Bratunac and the implications for the local area is that on the 18th -- and I haven't said this so far because I only remembered it later. On the 18th of October, I was summoned to Sarajevo urgently to attend a similar meeting, similar to the one of April 1991. It was a plenary meeting of the main board extended with all the presidents of the municipal boards in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was an extraordinary meeting, and I received the invitation from the SDS secretariat; I think I was summoned by telephone. I went there, and I attended the meeting which was chaired by the presidency of the SDS, and it was mainly Mr. Karadzic who spoke at the meeting. They commented on the well-known events of the assembly session of the 15th of October, and we were then given a set of documents that we were duty-bound to implement in our local areas. I'm not sure, but I will try to recall. It was the principles of organisation of the Serbian People in the newly-arisen political circumstances, or something like that. The most important content of that document was our obligations that we had to implement on the ground. That is, to prepare for a plebiscite of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina and a decision had been reached to hold it in November. The question was then told us whether the Serbs were in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia. This is all well known. Besides this, we were told to form crisis staffs, and this was the first time that we had been given political instructions to form crisis staffs in the municipalities. At the time, the name was the Crisis Staff of the Serbian People. It was not just political; the recommendation was that the crisis staffs should also include people who were not from the party, who were not party people, but eminent people in their local communities. The second, or rather the third obligation we were given was to organise public fora in our local communities to inform the population of key political events, especially those of the 15th of October, and to explain this to the people. And we were given very precise instructions as to what we were to explain. Our positions were well known: That this decision was unconstitutional, that we were deeply opposed to it, and that we were now self-organising, in a manner of speaking. I did implement these conclusions in Bratunac, and there are minutes to show this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To conclude before the break, am I right in believing that all this you just mentioned happened in the framework of that what in your factual basis you called Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic undertook steps to establish Serbian ethnic territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, please understand, our time is limited. Let's try to focus on the core issues that are relevant for the crime we are seized with, that's the attack on Glogova. I take it that already after the 15th of October, it was decided to implement crisis staffs. Could you briefly explain when exactly you became a member or head of Crisis Staff for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will reply to your question. The crisis staff was first referred to as the Crisis Staff of the Serbian People pursuant to the decision reached at this meeting of the 18th of October that I mentioned. And a day or two after that, we did establish the Crisis Staff of the Serbian People in Bratunac, and I became its president. In November, or rather in December, we established a second crisis staff upon instructions from the variant A and B which I will speak about. And this was the SDS Crisis Staff, which is what the order said. And then I became the president of this crisis staff. I wish only to add a sentence in connection with the events in October and the meeting in Sarajevo. Our instructions were to hold a public forum, and I wish to say that I did hold it in Bratunac and informed the population about the intentions of the Serbian leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The political and government leadership, I'm referring to the people in the joint organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. At that meeting, we were told that the policy of creating a Serbian state or entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina would continue, and that specific measures in this connection would be taken. This was the first time I had learned that a Serbian state was being established in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After this, I wish only to mention a session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held in November. I don't know the exact date, but I do know that several conclusions were reached, and the Serbian autonomous provinces established in the summer of 1991 were verified. I wish to mention that the Romanija and Birac area was verified, and the instructions that we were to form a special Birac autonomous province arrived in December. And the constituent assembly of the SAO Birac was held. I know the exact date today, on the 8th of January 1992. I wish to add that I was not involved in the preparations for this meeting, nor was I present at it. It was held at Sekovici. If there are questions, I know exactly who the leaders were, who were the elected leaders at that meeting. I would now like to talk about December. There was a meeting of the same type on the 23rd of December as the one that had been held before. The SDS main board and the presidents of the municipal boards. The assembly held a session on the 23rd of December, or rather, I think the 21st and 22nd of December, but we were invited earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting again. Before we touch upon the 23rd of December, let's focus on the 19th of December because here, in fact, we wanted you to give us some further informations not included yet in the factual basis. Who invited for this meeting? Who attended the meeting? Who took the floor? And who is - yeah - finally responsible for the invention of the variant A and variant B? And what was the final target of these variants A and variant B?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. On the 19th of December, we were summoned to a meeting of the SDS main board extended to include the presidents of the municipal boards. And as this was taking place in an atmosphere of preparations for the holding of the assembly, I know that at that meeting, the deputies in the Serbian Assembly were present, as well as the entire leadership, political - when I say political, I mean the SDS - and the government, and the meeting was chaired by Mr. Karadzic. I can list the members of the main board whom I knew at the time and the presidents of the main boards -- municipal boards. But I'm not sure they were all present. From the Birac region, I will tell you the ones I knew best. I was there. Mr. Zekic, the president of the municipal board in Srebrenica, Stanic, Mr. Milenko Stanic, the president of the Vlasenica municipal board Mr. Rajko Djukic who was in the executive board. And the president at the time, I'm not a hundred per cent sure. Brano Grujic, the president of the Zvornik municipal. Mr. Vlasic, the president of the Sekovici municipal board. I also knew several deputies. Some of them had parallel functions, like Mr. Zekic for instance. I know Dr. Novakovic from Bijeljina. He also attended this meeting. They were all bound to attend, but I'm not sure they were really all there because at that time I was not familiar with all the presidents of the SDS municipal boards. When I mentioned the political leadership, all the sessions were chaired by the SDS presidency. And as the members changed frequently, all I can say with any certainty is that the meeting was chaired by Mr. Karadzic. I said that I am sure I also saw Mr. Krajisnik, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, but I cannot say to what extent they were present at this meeting and involved in the work of the assembly. I assume that they were present on both occasions, and I know for certain that I saw them there. Mr. Karadzic spoke at the meeting and acquainted us with the materials we were to take home to our municipalities. The materials were marked. I'm not sure I can give you the exact titles, that they were measures for the organisation of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not certain of the official title of the document. And we were told that this material, which was marked strictly confidential, would be handed out to us after the meeting. This material was passed by the presidency of the SDS. That's what we were told. And it contained instructions for the actions of all those participating in the meeting, including us, the presidents of the municipal boards. I remember only some details in connection with the explanation of the variants A and B because President Karadzic, after the political part of the meeting, spoke with great precision about the instructions in documents A and B. I remember that he warned us that we should take this very seriously and that we should absolutely implement this on the ground, explaining that the political crisis had reached a high point, that armed conflict could break out. He warned us that we had to maintain connections with people on the ground in the municipalities, and that we were responsible for informing people of all the steps and decisions that the leadership of the Serbs decided on at any particular moment. I remember he told us that we had to maintain connections with every household, even if only by courier if there was no other way. He was, of course, referring exclusively to the Serbs who lived on the territories. After the meeting was completed, we were given the written documents, the ones that Mr. Karadzic had commented on at the meeting. And on my return to Bratunac, I held a session of the municipal board and told the municipal board about the standpoints of the SDS, the presidency of the SDS, and I opened up the floor for discussion. We consulted about what we could implement in the Bratunac Municipality with respect to these measures. Let me just add that the conditions in Bratunac were not such, or we were not able to implement all these measures. The measures are contained in two paragraphs, both variants A and B had two stages of organisation. The first stage which was introduced at once, and the second stage which would be introduced depending on the circumstances, and we would be informed about this in time. In the first stage of organisation in the field, certain measures were to be taken, the first of which was to establish SDS crisis staffs. According to an automatic procedure provided for in these documents, minority municipalities in which Serbs held less than 50 per cent of the power in the local government bodies, the president of the municipal board was to be the president of the crisis staff. In majority municipalities, this was to be the president of the municipality. And we followed this rule. Because in Bratunac we were understaffed, as this is a very small town, the same crisis staff that we had earlier established as the Crisis Staff of the Serbian People was transformed into the SDS Crisis Staff. And according to the instructions we were given, I became the president of the SDS Crisis Staff. This was specific, but all the people in the previous crisis staff were either members or sympathisers of the SDS. I don't want to go into all the measures envisioned by the first variant, but I would like to say that they contained certain measures, disciplinary measures, in the sense of convening daily meetings of crisis staffs and municipal boards. We were instructed -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, may I interrupt you in the interests of the time that we really can focus on the open questions. You already told us who, to the best of your recollection, was present at the meeting. May I ask, was there anybody else present you would recall? For example, Mr. Brdjanin, and who was the representative for the Prijedor area? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot answer that question. I don't remember whether I saw any of those people. At the time, I didn't even know any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And then was the variant A and variant B at that point in time already established, or was it discussed during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Variants A and B existed in a written form. President Karadzic commented on those measures based on the written material that we received at the end of the meeting. We received the material in sealed envelopes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I put a straightforward question to you: What was the final goal of this adopted strategy? We all are aware of the six strategic goals adopted the 12th of May 1992. Was already at this point in time a discussion on the final goals of the implementation of variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, it was explained to us that a state would be formed. I don't remember whether at the time we used the term "entity." The Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we were told that these were measures of the self-organising of the Serbian People in extraordinary circumstances and special circumstances. We were not told at the meeting whether this had anything to do with the documents which were drafted and published later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the factual basis, one can read something about - that you already mentioned - strictly confidential instructions, but also use is made of the term affirmative actions, policy relating to the use of force, or the objectives set forth by the Bosnian Serb leadership. Could you please explain the development to this "affirmative actions," factual basis, paragraph 12, or "the policy relating to the use of force" in the factual basis, paragraph 13?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This meeting, and in variants A and B, provided for measures of separation, institutional division of the organs of authority in the municipalities. This was particularly problematic in minority communities where the Serbs were a minority, there was no way to resolve this in an institutional way, but there were suggestions that this should be done unilaterally and that parallel Serb organs of authority should be formed in minority municipalities. In areas where the Serbs were a majority, this does not present a problem. It was a problem only in Serb minority municipalities. I would like to discuss this question. I believe today, I know it for sure, that those measures were a continuity of the SDS's policy from the spring of 1991 aimed at creating Serb ethnic territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina which later, in a period, also included violent or forceful methods. I'm talking now about December 1991. I did not have any information, neither was I told, that these political steps and this strategy would include such methods. I had the opportunity to see this later. And today, I know that these methods were -- these violent methods were a part of the strategy to create Serb ethnic territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and tell us a little bit more what you mean when pleading guilty to the sentence that "Miroslav Deronjic" - as it is said in paragraph 12 - "took positive and concrete actions, including affirmative actions, and related to the use of force to remove non-Serbs from Serb-designated territories." What do you mean by "use of force"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 5th of May 1992, in a conversation with Mr. Zekic, I found out that besides all of the plans which never explicitly contained the use of force, that use of force was planned and that it was already being implemented in neighbouring municipalities. Of course, violent methods were already beginning to be used in Bratunac and Srebrenica. From that point on, the 5th of May 1992, I knew that those methods were a component part of the plans for creating the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Deronjic because he has a copy of that document in Serbian, so he can open that document in front of him, and then he can give the comments, if that is the wishes of the Trial Chamber, in order to save time, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If it could assist us in coming more expeditiously to this term "use of force," what it envisaged, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I also make another suggestion to the Court. If Mr. Deronjic does not have before him a copy of a factual basis, Your Honour refers to specific paragraphs, it might be of benefit to Mr. Deronjic if he had a copy of the paragraphs in front of him so he can read them and put them in the proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. I refer to paragraph 13 of the factual basis. And by the way, whilst Mr. Deronjic is reading, may I take it that when marrying the indictment with the factual basis, the fundamentum of our case is the indictment. And Mr. Deronjic has pleaded guilty to the indictment in its entirety without any reservation. So therefore, I take it that, for example, in number 2 -- number 1 and number 2, when we have additional factual basis for the purposes of the judgement, we can take this additional factual bases also as accepted and included, and we need not go into details of these questions. So that we regard, for example, paragraphs 10 through 13 only as additional factual bases for the purposes of the judgement. Is this acceptable for the parties? Then we would only need to have some clarification where the indictment in itself might have a discrepancy or if there is a real discrepancy between indictment and factual basis. Can we proceed this way in order to proceed as expeditious as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Certainly it is the indictment itself that is controlling in this case. The factual basis provides facts that support the plea of guilty, but it is the indictment itself that is controlling in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yeah. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification. This facilitates our work. And then we are still with paragraph 12 and 13 of the factual basis for our better understanding of the terms, the relatively vague terms used there "affirmative actions" and "the use of force to remove non-Serbs." What would this include, "the use of force"? Apparently it's based on the aforementioned strictly confidential instructions - correct? - given to you on or about the 19th of December 1991. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In paragraph 12 that I took specific and decisive actions in order to support the steps from variants A and B, this includes certain steps undertaken in this sense in the municipality of Bratunac. Here, what is meant is that the measure of the division of the police in Bratunac, I implemented it in the local, common joint assembly in Bratunac together with the representatives of the SDA, and that we have a record of that, minutes of that, and a document which was drafted after that assembly session. I also undertook some other actions, but because of the specific nature of the situation in Bratunac, some of those instructions from variants A and B could not be implemented. And by that, I mean, the formation of special courts of Serbs as an institution; also, separate police stations in certain areas; the separation of all the possible organs of power and the institutions of power in general. As far as paragraph 13 is concerned, it states "and later, to the use of force." I understand that to mean what is contained in the factual basis, or in my interview, that on the 5th of May I unequivocally found out that the use of force is also one of the methods in order to implement these objectives, and that is how I acted regarding the events in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what were these means of use of force? Could you elaborate a little bit more on this because there's a huge range how you can use -- make use of force, with making use of weapons including -- or whatever. I don't want to anticipate your answer. So please, if you could tell us a little bit more what the term "use of force" includes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Q The term "use of force" includes violent transfer of population -- of the population from those territories and includes conduct -- the conduct of the volunteer units which are already arrived in the area, and the conduct of the Yugoslav People's Army in those events, and the conduct of the crisis staffs and individuals on the Serb side during that period. So the term "use of force" in my opinion is used in this sense and in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it includes the conduct of the volunteer units which are already -- had arrived in the area, and the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it include the use of arms, the use of a tank?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it include the killing of people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. Members of the Muslim ethnic group were killed in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this formed part of the plan. And may I ask, was it already envisaged in these documents called strictly confidential instructions to make use of this force even amounting to killing of people? Was it already envisaged in the plans in December?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was not explicitly stated, nor implied, and we were not given such instruments out in the field relating to the use of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So who finally decided about the use of force and the degree of use of force? We are now already in the middle of the events leading to the 9th of May. And what actually was your concrete role?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I found out about the use of force before this event, earlier, and prior to my conversation with Mr. Zekic. I could clearly see and follow the events in Bijeljina, the events in Zvornik, which are municipalities that are very close to us in the territorial sense. Zvornik borders on the Bratunac Municipality. The events began on the 1st of April and continued throughout April. These events are well known, so I do not want to take your time regarding these events. During that time, I drew certain conclusions about the use of force in Bijeljina and Zvornik, and in some other municipalities about which I found out through the media. I found out about the use of force through the media in those municipalities. My main conclusion was that those paramilitary units were units known as Arkan's Guard, White Eagles, or other volunteers from Serbia. These units were sent to these regions from Serbia and they used force against the Muslim population in that area, and that the final or ultimate objective of such conduct was to expel the non-Serb population from those municipalities. So I did have the opportunity to monitor these the events in Eastern Bosnia and Podrinje, which are municipalities close to us and with a similar population makeup as us. So my conclusion was that the operative part - and when I say the operative part or the operational part, I mean the actual implementation of the use of force - I concluded that this was directed from Belgrade. And my final conclusion from a conversation with Mr. Zekic on the 5th of May, I found out that this was a part of the plan and that the Bosnian Serb leadership was also behind this, and that also includes President Karadzic and all the other political representatives of Bosnian Serbs. This was something that was agreed upon with the Serbian leadership, and that the implementation of these methods out in the field was underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's go back to Glogova. You mentioned already as paramilitary units, Arkan's Guard. And just for the record of this case, who is the person behind the White Eagles? Would you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found out later, people are mentioning Mr. Jovic, Mr. Jovic. I can't remember his first name now. He was the organiser of the units known as the White Eagles, and this was a small opposition party in Serbia. And when I say "opposition," this should be understood as being said in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the next slight discrepancy. In the indictment, paragraph 20, I take it that you have already also the indictment before you in B/C/S? Is it correct? Paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment, it reads that "The municipality was taken over by Bosnian Serb forces on the 17th of April 1992." In the factual basis, it reads, "On the 17th of April 1992, volunteers from the SFRY entered Bratunac, and at the Hotel Fontana their commander met with and issued an ultimatum to the leaders of Srebrenica and Bratunac Muslim communities to surrender weapons and legal authority to Bosnian Serbs or suffer destruction at the hands of thousands of Serb soldiers," and so on. So was it a joint action of Bosnian Serb forces together with the volunteers, or how shall we understand it? You know best what happened at that time and who was responsible for this taking over.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will reply to your question. Mr. Zekic brought the volunteers to Bratunac. I was not involved in their arrival in Bratunac in any way. I attended the meeting at Fontana because I had been invited to come there. And I wish to enter a minor correction. We're talking about the meeting that had already started in the Fontana Hotel on the 17th of April 1992. And when I arrived, only the representatives of the Muslims from Srebrenica were there. The members of the volunteer units and the political leadership, or rather the leadership of the SDS from Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found Mr. Simic there at the meeting, and he was at that time president of the Serbian Assembly in Bratunac. And he left the meeting very soon. I wish to say that there were no representatives of the Muslims from Bratunac there. But I was told at the meeting that they were to be given an ultimatum about abandoning power in Bratunac. The takeover of power referred to the public security station in Bratunac, and this was carried out by the volunteers after the Muslim representatives and the chief of the security station and a large number of policemen, after my conversation with them, left the public security station in Bratunac and set off in the direction of Tuzla. No unit or individual from Bratunac participated in this, Your Honour. I know this for certain. I was there, and I remember all the images. I remember a man. I think he was a policeman, an ethnic Muslim, who was just sitting on the stairs when they entered the public security station. They stayed there for about half an hour. They collected documents, stamps. They took the vehicles that the public security station had. And after that, together with Goran Zekic and the other members of that group, they went off to Srebrenica. This is what I feel is a brief report about this event. If, of course, you have any questions, I'm ready to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the role you played in this meeting in your own capacity? Did you act on the same footing together with your colleague, Mr. Zekic, or were there any other persons leading the takeover? Who is finally responsible? And I recall, and I have to give you the hint that you already pleaded guilty to this point. But we have to clarify what was your relationship to the volunteers. You accepted the arrival of the volunteers and their involvement in the use of force, as you just a few minutes ago told us. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I attended this meeting. I was summoned to that meeting. I stayed there for a very brief time because I had been invited by the Muslim representatives who asked me to come to the public security station, and they said they wanted to talk to me. I have stated exactly what they asked me; that is, the representatives of the Bosnian Muslims. They asked me for guarantees that these volunteers would not do anything to them. I responded that I had never seen them before, I didn't know them, and I was unable to provide any guarantees to the Muslim representatives. They asked me if they could leave Bratunac, and they asked me to help them leave safely. I said I would do everything to help them leave safely, and I have already quoted the questions they asked me and my replies. I participated in that meeting only briefly because the central topic at that meeting were relations in Srebrenica. Why representatives of the Muslims from Bratunac were not present who had been given an ultimatum is something I can only guess at. I can only assume that these people were afraid to attend the meeting. I went to the station and talked to them, and they expressed the wish to leave Bratunac. I did not oppose this in any way, nor did I have any instruments to guarantee their security at that moment. At that time, I had no executive function in the Bratunac Municipality except that I was the president of the SDS Bratunac Crisis Staff. These are the facts that I have set out and that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me ask you directly. Did you order the disarmament of Glogova by the end of April, beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The decision on the disarming of the Muslims in the villages of Bratunac was made by the JNA, by Mr. Reljic after the JNA arrived in Bratunac. I think this was sometime after the 20th of April. The meeting at which he made this decision was held in a company in Bratunac called Vihor Bratunac. He made this decision there, and it's a well-known fact that at that time Mr. Reljic introduced a military government in Bratunac, and he informed the population of this by putting up posters in Bratunac saying that he was the commander of Bratunac and he was taking responsibility for events in Bratunac. At a later date, and let me mention that the disarming of the Muslim population in Bratunac started on the day his decision was made; that is, the 23rd or the 24th of April probably, because in Glogova there was already disarming on the 27th. And at his orders, there had been disarming of the village of Pocus [phoen], and I had participated in this as a soldier since I had been mobilised by the Territorial Defence. At one of the crisis staff meetings in this period, Mr. Reljic, the captain of this unit, brought a decision to the crisis staff on the disarming of Muslims, and he asked us to confirm it, which we did. However, the decision on disarming itself is something I was not able to tell him about, nor did he ask me about it. He did this when he arrived in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So when do you believe one can call Glogova a disarmed and undefended town? From which point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I would say with great certainty that this would be the 27th of April because all the witness testimonies speak about this. This is when the largest amount of weapons was collected, and I think the disarming action lasted two or three days, since Glogova is a large village. This was done by JNA units, units of the Territorial Defence, and the police, and I knew about these activities. As I said, it was in this period or a day or two later that we approved what they were doing, and one might say that in early May, Glogova had already been disarmed completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's now turn to the actual attack on Glogova. And here we can read in the indictment, paragraph 8(e), that - and you pleaded guilty to this already - that "Miroslav Deronjic in his capacity as the president of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bratunac, a position which gave him de facto and de jure control over the TO, and de facto control over the police in the Municipality of Bratunac gave an order to attack the village of Glogova, burn part of it down, and forcibly displace its Bosnian Muslim residents." Correct? You stick to that what you have pleaded guilty to already?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All this is completely correct. I stand by this, and I have no comment to make on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To whom did you give the order to attack?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 8th in the evening at the session of the crisis staff, I gave the order to attack to the Bratunac Territorial Defence, including the police forces in Bratunac. I was unable to command the JNA units. I only asked them whether they would participate in this. And Mr. Reljic, the commander of this unit, told me they would participate in this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the volunteers and their participation in the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to say that at that time, we had certain clashes with the volunteers. I personally had several clashes with the volunteers, and there were certain decisions about their expulsion. Unfortunately, the population disagreed with this, and the army took control of this with their arrival in Bratunac. None of these volunteers attended the crisis staff meeting, and my decision stands in relation to them. I don't know to what extent. I do know that they did participate in this action in Glogova, and that is something I could talk about with greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could be so kind and elaborate a little bit more on this, especially in relation to paragraph 35 of the factual basis where you plead guilty to already that you yourself urged Captain Reljic to fire a tank shell into a house at the initial stage of the attack in order to sow panic amongst the residents of Glogova. If you could, in context, elaborate a little bit more on the development and what actually occurred at this point in time, the evening of the 8th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All this is completely true. At this meeting, I asked Mr. Reljic to take decisive action in this attack. I will try to explain my reasons for this. Before this, I had had talks with Mr. Zekic, and he told me that violent methods had been agreed upon and that they were already being used in a number of municipalities. The decision to attack Glogova was a result of this information. The decision was confirmed by the other side, and by this I mean Serbia. In Bratunac at the time there was a member of the Serbian State Security whose name was Predrag Spasojevic. He turned up in Bratunac in mid-April. I asked him what his service thought of my intention, as it was then, to forcibly remove the population of Glogova and the centre of Bratunac, including two suburbs. He said that he had contacted his service and that he thought that this decision was correct and that I had confirmation that my way of thinking was acceptable. It was not clear what the role of the JNA was to be in this, although on the 7th of May I had a meeting with Mr. Reljic. At his invitation, we went to look down from a certain vantage point, that is my native village, to see what all of Glogova looked like. On that occasion, we agreed that the attack was to be launched over the next few days in Bratunac. But during these meetings, he always said that I was not competent to give orders to his unit and that he would contact his command and consult them. His command was in Sekovici as far as I knew, which was where the entire mechanised brigade was, and I never went there, nor did I know the people there. I thought that what he said was reasonable. At the meeting of the crisis staff, I asked whether they would participate. He answered yes, but he left this open by saying that he would consult his command about this. I asked him if he did participate in the attack in the first stage because I didn't know what we would run into in Glogova. Glogova is a really enormous village. So I asked that the army take an active role rather than simply observing. At the meeting, I proposed to him that in the first stage when we get to Glogova, he should fire a shell at a building in Glogova. The reason was to let the Muslims know that the JNA's directly on our side. This would give us an advantage in the attack and sow fear and panic among the Muslim population, and also break down any ambitions they might have had to resist us in this attack. As far as I know, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. When ordering this tank shell on a house, you accepted and you took into account that this house might be -- that there might be persons living in this house, and shelling a house would cause the risk that people living in this house be killed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to give a small clarification. Yes, I did not issue an order. I made a recommendation. I don't want to justify myself when I say that. I suggested this to an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who trained his whole life for his job. I believe that he also had to take care about the manner in which he would use that shell. In my interview to the Prosecution, I didn't really discuss this topic very much, but I am sure that we all understood, and I provided an explanation, to the extent that there was firing at a facility which need not necessarily be a house. He could have fired the shell at a stable or a barn or some kind of auxiliary building. So I perhaps even said that. I clarified this when we discussed it. I also felt that he was responsible for not using the shell in the wrong way and in order not to jeopardise human lives. Luckily, he did not accept this proposal. This grenade shell was not fired. I think that he acted in a soldierly manner, and in my opinion, this was quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in the hearing the 30th of September, you accepted without any reservation that, I quote: "Miroslav Deronjic urged Captain Reljic to fire a tank shell into a house at the initial stage of the attack in order to sow panic amongst the Muslims residents of Glogova." Do you want to withdraw this, or do you stand by that what you have pleaded guilty to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I am not withdrawing a single word from this quote, but I did provide a certain clarification. And if Your Honours -- you may or may not consider the explanation as relevant, but I do stand by what I said at the crisis staff meeting in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that you urged Captain Reljic? Let's do it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
