utterances.text: I could say that I reiterated this several times to see whether he was prepared to actively participate in that operation and whether he would take an active part in the operation, because there was a dilemma about that. I will tell you something that I did not tell the Prosecution as additional information. There was also one of his deputies who was present there who said at a certain point, "Yes, the army will participate, Mr. Deronjic," and he addressed the members of the crisis staff. "The army will take part in this," and this is when we finished the discussion on this topic, after he gave an answer to this question of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you stand by your guilty plea that you urged Captain Reljic. And this is the same Mr. Reljic, and now I come to another document, the interview either of October or, as Mr. Harmon said, November - unfortunately we can't find any date on this document - page 30, paragraph 101. And there it, reads, I quote: "At one of the sessions of the crisis staff, Mr. Reljic told us that he made a decision to disarm Muslim villages. He called this campaign a campaign to disarm extremists, but we knew that it pertained to Muslim villages. This campaign was conducted in the following manner: First, the TO would be mobilised. And then very early in the morning before dawn, they would surround the village but make a broad circle, not get too close to the houses in the village, and then he would give the signal and perhaps one or two bullets would be fired by each soldier." This is correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's, then, continue. Mr. Reljic and you were aware - this is my conclusion; correct me, please, if I am wrong - that you had in front of you a disarmed and undefended village. However, you urged Captain Reljic, quote again, "to fire a tank shell into a house at the initial stage of the attack"? When shelling a house, whatever house it may be, isn't it true that you, in ordering this, you accept that a foreseeable consequence might be that a person is inside this house and would be killed by this shelling? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm referring to the transcript of this session, and at 17:18:14, you referred to this quote, this passage, you read as being in paragraph 101, page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The paragraph, copy of the statement that I have in English, has that quote in paragraph 102. So I'm not sure what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present this document we have -- no, I have my copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It appears to be an identical paragraph, numbered differently. So we will have to regulate that later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Please, the correct document will be signed later. So okay. We reached this step. And could you then, please, continue. What about your own - please, and in your own words - what actually did you do on the evening of the 8th of May until the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Your Honour, are you thinking about what I did after the meeting was finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: After the meeting concluded, the meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff at which we made the decision to attack the village of Glogova, I went home very quickly to change. I think I'm almost sure of that, and I joined a unit of the Territorial Defence which was lined up in front of the municipal building. The unit was commanded by Mr. Miloje Bozic. He was unfortunately killed. I joined that unit because that was a TO unit to which I am assigned to. Anyway, the unit's assignment was to enter the village of Glogova at night -- in the area of Srebrenica. This area is the area of Srebrenica, and Potocari is exclusively inhabited by Muslims. Our objective was to look out and try to prevent any attempt of escape from the village of Glogova and to prevent anybody from Srebrenica coming and trying to enter Glogova and trying to surprise our forces in any way. If I'm not mistaken, I went with that unit at about 1000 hours. I know the road that we took. We took a village road. This is not really a proper road. These are just small village paths. We went behind the village of Glogova on the south side and set up groups of soldiers at certain elevations around there, including myself. Mr. Miloje Bozic assigned who would be in what group and where the group would be positioned. I was instructed to remain at one post. I obeyed that order and I stayed there. We remained there until dawn on the 9th of May. Nothing happened during the night. We were at a safe distance from the village of Glogova. But it was possible to have a good view of the whole of Glogova from that elevation. In the morning, at about 6.00 in the morning, we noticed, and this was in accordance with what we had agreed, that Serb forces were starting to go into Glogova. The best place or the best thing that we could see was the road from Bratunac. We could see that at a safe distance, they were stopping vehicles, trucks, and buses. There were -- it was prearranged for them to be there so that they could transport the population towards Kladanj. We saw that the attack or the entrance of our forces to Glogova was taking part from all directions as agreed. And in that -- at that stage, I noticed that our forces were entering Glogova first from the north, and some buildings were already torched there. Our conduct, the conduct of the soldiers who were with me at the time and who were around me, was such -- it was in accordance with the orders that we had, and that was to stand still and not to do anything, not to make any moves. Miloje Bozic was touring the lines. At one point I asked him to give me the hand-held radio that he had - it's a walkie-talkie; I don't know exactly what the name is - so that I could get in touch with somebody to see what was going on in Glogova. I noticed that the houses were being torched in a much larger number than was agreed at a meeting of the crisis staff. I contacted the other side with -- over the prearranged channel. Mr. Bozic turned the hand-held radio on for me. I spoke to Mr. Predrag Spasojevic. I asked him, "What is happening in Glogova, are things proceeding the way we agreed?" We could hear shooting. We were about 2 kilometres from the village, or maybe a little less. Perhaps we were a kilometre, 1 kilometre from the village. He said that everything was going well, that there were no problems because he was in contact with those who were leading the units. I did not comment on the excessive torching, and that is how I ended my conversation with him. In the centre of Glogova itself, besides this person, the commander of the TO was there, Captain Reljic as well, and I saw that the tanks were in the centre of Glogova, or to be precise, it was one tank and three armoured transporter vehicles. I could see that they were in the centre of Glogova. The entry of the forces into the village was not visible because that is the terrain. It's not possible to see it. But the torching was something that was visible, and I already said that I did not make any comments about that. At 9.00, as far as I recall, I think that it was at 9.00, we received the order that our task there is finished, that our units had entered Glogova, and that they were forcibly bringing the population to the centre of the village. I could see that our transport vehicles intended to bring them over to Kladanj had arrived in the centre of Glogova. The order for us was that we should go to a crossroads, taking an old macadam road which would not take us to Glogova. So we did that from the south side, and then we would go back to Bratunac. So we set off on this old macadam road which leads from Bratunac to Kravica, which is behind Glogova. Kravica is a Serbian village. We went down this macadam road, and we reached the area of Avdagina Njiva, so we came on to the asphalt road which passes straight through the village of Glogova. This is also an area which is not actually physically part of the village of Glogova. This is where I encountered a unit from Kravica. Across this road, I noticed that none of those people who were there had entered the village of Glogova. We talked a little bit about the operation. I knew some people well from Kravica, Raso Milosevic who was the commander of the unit, and Jovan Nikolic who was a member of the municipal board of the SDS. I spoke with them. They were not satisfied over the burning of the village, and allegedly that was the reason why they did not go into the village. Later, I found out that a part of their unit did get into the village of Glogova from the area of Halilovici. I did not say that during this move -- I apologise to the interpreters. I skipped saying that while we were moving from the place where we were when we came down to this macadam road which was directly below us, there were several Muslim houses there. The soldiers who were around me entered those houses in order to check if anyone was inside. At that point, one of the houses was torched. The other soldiers asked me what should they do with the rest of the houses? There were about three or four houses there. And I said that I approved that they should burn them. I agreed that they should burn them. We continued down this field, and I met a group of people there. I knew one of the people there. He was commanding a platoon. His name is Nedjo. I can't remember his last name. His nickname is Djedura. He was deep in the rear in a wood, and he was well known for some extreme incidents in the prewar period. So I was a little bit provocative about those things. And I think he was here, he was pretending to be very brave. And I ordered him to torch several houses that were there in the area. And I wanted to check if he would do that, and he did do that. They burnt a few homes -- houses that were there. After I left for Avdagina Njiva, Your Honour, I stayed for a short while with the people I mentioned. And then I went off to Bratunac. My intention was to arrive at the funeral of Mr. Zekic who had been killed on the 8th of May. I passed through the village of Glogova. And I can say now with some certainty that I was given a list in a private car, that arrived in the Fontana Hotel. On the way through the village of Glogova, I noticed a large number of people gathered in the centre of Glogova. I observed our buses there. I observed the presence of the army, the police; that is, the Bratunac police. I can't tell you exactly whom I saw, but they were there in the centre of the village. I did not notice anything that would indicate that things were happening beyond what we had agreed at the crisis staff meeting, which was that all the residents of Glogova without exception should be collected together and taken off in the direction of Kladanj. I went to the Fontana Hotel. Before that, I think I stopped at the morgue in the health centre in Bratunac and that I was present when Mr. Zekic's body was being prepared for burial. Then I went back to Fontana because we had agreed that a ceremony for Mr. Zekic should be held there because his family had decided that he was to be buried in Serbia, in a place called Ljubovija. This is the neighbouring municipality in Serbia. His father, his wife, and his children had decided that. In front of the Fontana Hotel, we were to say good-bye to the corpse of Mr. Zekic, and it was agreed that I, as the president of the crisis staff, should hold an obituary speech. I didn't do that. I asked, I think, Mr. Tesic, to do it because I said that I was in a very emotional state, as Mr. Zekic had been a close friend, and that I was unable to give the obituary. After that, the procession set out. I can't be very precise, but I think it was in the afternoon of that day. And we set out in the direction of Ljubovija. In this procession, we attended the church ceremony and the burial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the interests of time, may I interrupt you here because this is not part of our case. You already went one step further touching upon the events of the 9th of May. And we should really focus on that crimes that were committed this very day. A very direct question: Was it already in advance when you planned the meeting held beforehand? Was it already planned to burn and destroy the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Categorically, nobody mentioned the mosque. This was not even discussed. When I passed through Glogova, it was not destroyed. My information indicates that it was destroyed on the 9th of May in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: By whom? Who did destroy the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My information, and I'm really not absolutely certain, is that it was blown up, that it was dynamited by volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you regard this as a foreseeable consequence of the attack against Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, really, I must say that in the context of everything that happened, I should have foreseen such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the aforementioned document of in all likelihood November 2003, on page 31, in my copy, it's paragraph 106, you stated, I quote: "As a result of the attack on the village of Glogova on the 9th of May 1992, 65 Bosnian Muslims, residents of the village, were murdered; the entire Bosnian Muslim population of the village was forcibly displaced; and a substantial number of Bosnian Muslim residences in Glogova were razed to the ground." This is absolutely in line with both the indictment and the factual basis you pleaded guilty to. However, may I also, with respect to these 65 killings, and you will recall that we heard the names of these 65 dead persons, that this murder of 65 Bosnian Muslims was a foreseeable result of the attack, and you took into account and accepted that this might happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I state that that is so and that the way that is put is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please understand that for legal reasons, I have to come back to the one or other point. Until now, we discussed more or less the objective part of all the acts, but now we have to discuss those parts in the indictment and the factual basis where your state of mind at that point in time was discussed. And I wonder what the meaning in paragraph 8 of the indictment and paragraph 18 of the factual basis is that -- here it reads: "Miroslav Deronjic, exercising de facto and de jure control of the president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff over the TO and the de facto control of the Bratunac police forces, authorised the TO and Bratunac police forces to disarm the Bosnian Muslim population in Glogova." And in the factual basis, it also reads that you authorised the TO to disarm the Bosnian Muslim population. You will understand the question in the light of your previous answer that in fact, the disarmament was ordered by others. And you mentioned concrete names. So how shall we understand that you authorised the disarmament?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood the charges in the indictment as a fact that is derived from a decision with which we agreed. When I say "we," I'm thinking of the crisis staff in a period when Mr. Reljic brought this decision and asked us to declare ourselves affirmatively on the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in other words, you joined this mission to disarm the population of Glogova. You not only accepted it, but also endorsed it in your capacity, in all your capacities you had at this point in time in Glogova. Is this a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the decision to approve this operation was reached later when the disarming of the Glogova village was completed. If you're thinking of my personal position at that point in time, I was there nearby when the operation was being carried out. I took part in it personally, and I did not oppose the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's time for a break now. Maybe it's a good opportunity for you to discuss with your counsel this question. I have to come back to this because it still remains unclear what the term "authorised the disarmament" means in this context. So I will come back to this question immediately after the break. The trial stays adjourned until a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I come back directly to paragraph 8 of the indictment and 18 of the factual basis. Could you please explain what does it mean when you said "authorised to disarm."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will give an explanation. I said that at a meeting of the crisis staff we authorised the decision on the disarmament of Muslims in Bratunac. In that way, we agreed with that operation, accepted it as our own, accepted it as justified for the period when it was implemented. In that way, I, as the president of the crisis staff, and the crisis staff accepted the decision as our own. And in that sense do I mean that we authorised it and that I authorised in that way Captain Reljic to carry out his action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. May we now turn to paragraph 8(d) and paragraph 19 of the factual basis. It's only a slight question. This the indictment, it reads, and you pleaded guilty to this: "Milosevic added that he was speaking on behalf of Miroslav Deronjic," whereas in the factual basis you can only read that Milutin Milosevic told the villagers of Glogova they would not be attacked because they had turned over their weapons. Did Milosevic speak as it reads in the indictment on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not present in Glogova. I accepted the facts as cited by the Prosecution, that he said that on my behalf. But I cannot say exactly what happened there. I accept that statement, and I believe that it is possible, and I accepted it in this sense. I never discussed this with him, but I accept that he may have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you were absolutely in agreement what Milosevic has said. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. I accepted all of those actions, and I agreed with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And also, in relation to your state of mind, coming back to the question of the volunteers, we already, I think, have found an acceptable conclusion on this. It reads in paragraph 36 of the factual basis that you coordinated and monitored the attack on Glogova. Do you stand by your plea?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think as for the next paragraphs in this document, we need not go into further details because you have already testified on this. Could you, then, please, in conclusion tell us what happened immediately after you had been in Glogova. By the way, did you see persons in Glogova that had been killed during the attack when you came to the town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I state that I did not see nor did I knew at that point in time anything about that, and that is really true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please, then, proceed. What happened this 9th of -- later, this 9th of May, the 10th, and 11th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order not to repeat what I did in the afternoon and in the evening of that day, I would like to conclude, after Goran Zekic's funeral, we met because the majority of the crisis staff members attended the funeral. We met at an unofficial meeting. We didn't even take the minutes of it, but we did discuss the situation in Glogova, about what happened in Glogova. The central topic and what we knew at that time was that Glogova was torched to an extent that was not planned or meant. We discussed the killings [as interpreted]. To this very day, I would like to say that we, or I personally, did not have any information about these killings. During this meeting, this conversation, it was agreed that I should inform Mr. Reljic that in the future actions, any kind of torching of houses should be banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is a misinterpretation in the transcript. 69:7. It says "we discussed the killings" and I believe our client said "we did not discuss the killings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. May it be please corrected page 69, line 7. "We discussed not the killings." The "not" has to be included. So then the 10th of May. Do you recall any special events on the 10th of May in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The operation, as was agreed at the crisis staff meeting on the 9th of May, continued by inviting the Muslim population, which remained in Bratunac at the time, to come to designated places, and that the police and the military would transport them in the direction of Kladanj. This was the agreement of the 9th of May reached at the same meeting of the crisis staff that we mentioned. At one point at the stadium, which was one of the locations where the people were supposed to come, I was informed that there was separations of men and women in the group of Muslims who had come to the stadium. Together with the president of the executive board who informed me about this, Rodoljub Djukanovic, I went to the stadium to check what this was all about. This was my first indication of such acts. I came to the stadium. I didn't meet anybody from the army there. I saw a large group of volunteers, and Mr. Predrag Cubrilo, who was their commander. I saw a group of Muslims who were separated, men, they were standing along the wall of the stadium. I asked him what this was all about. Then there was an argument. I insisted that he should explain to me why this was being done, and he said this was an order of the army and these people would be exchanged for some Serbs. I went, after that conversation which was quite heated, to the police station. I asked the police commander -- the police station commander to see what he could do about this. I met Luka Bogdanovic who at the time was the duty of the commander of the police station in Bratunac, and he told me there are no police officers in Bratunac, that they were all out in the field, that they are inviting people to come to these certain places as we had agreed. I returned to the crisis staff, to the municipal building, and I was summoned to Pale. I don't remember how I got this information. Somebody told me that I was being summoned to go to Pale in relation to some meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but let's stay for a moment in Bratunac. I think you would -- you will agree that the word "that they had invited the Muslims to come to certain points, especially the stadium," is a diplomatic description of ordering these people to come to the stadium and other locations. Correct? And are you aware and is it correct that some of those people, in fact, were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're absolutely right. I used that term in a technical sense. Summoned or invited via police loudspeakers, but it was actually an order for them to come, and this was actually a forcible transportation of people from Bratunac and the surrounding suburbs. I am aware that those people were separated to the stadium during the night, and then they were taken to a hangar close to the -- near the Vuk Karadzic school. When I came back during the day, I found out that there was a large number of people there, about 500 people there, who had been placed in this hangar. If you think that it is necessary to discuss this topic further, I will continue. But what I wanted to say was on the 10th, I went to Pale, and I wanted to give you a chronological explanation of what happened. But I will do it in whatever way you see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could, please, first explain what is your knowledge about the killing of some of those people ordered to come to the stadium and other locations.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I returned from Pale, the next day I was informed that these people who were separated at the hangar were abused, that volunteers were going there, as well as some local citizens. I said in my interview that I found out that the father of Goran Zekic went there, Drago Zekic, and that he was conducting investigations about his son. I was told that people were taken out of the hangar, taken in an unknown direction, and that they never came back. In the course of that day, we took a series of measures to prevent this from happening. And I will mention a few things which I've already said during my talks with the investigators. I said that I spoke with the commander of the paramilitary unit, that he told me that he was not quite informed about the situation - of course, he wasn't telling the truth - and that he would try to prevent his units from entering there. I went to see the military police which was formed -- which was formed by Mr. Reljic. I did not see him in Bratunac to that day, and to this day I cannot actually tell you what this is all about and where he was on that day. We also asked for the help of one of our local units, that it should also try to prevent the things that were going on at the hangar. We received a promise that some of them would try to prevent this. I spoke also with the commander of the military police, Mr. Savo Babic, and he said that he would do everything to prevent what was going on there and that he would step up the security around the hangar. The next day, this is already on the 12th, these actions continued. I received information that somebody saw some killed people in the Drina River, that they had been thrown into the river. I asked to go and see this for myself. I went to that location just underneath, below the bridge, and I did see several bodies in the river. I returned to the crisis staff, and we continued to discuss what we could do. On the 12th in the evening, between the 12th and the 13th, we held a meeting of the crisis staff, and that evening we agreed on some measures which we could implement at the time. We decided to release all the people who had remained alive from the hangar and to transport them to Pale, to the municipality where our Serbian leadership was at the time. During the night, after midnight, with the help of the local police, the local civilian police and the military police, we released all of those people. We boarded them on trucks with tarpaulins. We made a list of all the survivors who happened to be in the hangar at the time, and we took them to Pale and handed them over. The order was that their handover should be confirmed in writing when they were handed over to Pale. And I do have that document. The second decision that we made or adopted on the 13th of May 1992 related to the volunteers whom we blamed for the majority of the killings that happened at the hangar. We decided to expel all the volunteers from Bratunac, and also a decision to expel Reljic, whom we blamed for the separation of people in the first place and for them having been placed in this area, which made it possible for all of these killings to take place. These decisions were implemented partially, not in whole, because the next day already a vast mass of people gathered led by the local extremists, and these events are well known in Bratunac, when they physically broke into the municipal building and physically attacked the members of the crisis staff. In reference to those whom we found who had been killed in the hangar, I instructed for the military medical services to be called. I got in touch with Stankovic from Belgrade. I asked him to bring a team of experts so we could identify those bodies and to help us to bury those people in the proper way. And the next day or in the course of that same day, he did come. He examined all the bodies, established their identity. They were marked, and they were placed in these nylon bodybags as regulations require. They were given ID numbers, and they were buried in a mass grave publicly in the middle of the day. We had even ordered some Muslim tombstones for them according to the Muslim tradition, but it was then thought that this could possibly have been interpreted as a provocative action by the extremists. So as far as I know when I was arrested, those tombstones were still in the public utilities warehouse, so they were never used. So I did give a broad explanation of all of these events in a previous interview. And if you have questions, Your Honours, I would be happy to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is your estimate, now reviewing these events, how many people were killed in your municipality between the 8th and the 12th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you said between the 8th? Does this include Glogova, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accepted the facts put forward by the Office of the Prosecutor as to the number of people killed in Glogova. I wish to say that neither today nor at the time did I have any precise information about the number of people who had been killed. I have no reason to doubt that the figure of 65 mentioned by the Office of the Prosecutor is correct, and I accept this fact. As for the people killed in the hangar, I wish to say that at one point in my interview, without checking this previously, I mentioned a number which is not correct. I truly hope it is not correct. I said about 200 people had been killed. But on my return to Bratunac, I asked a person who could give me precise information and who had done the postmortems and burials of these people, a person called Aleksandar Tesic from the military, and he told me that this number was incorrect and that he had information about this and that it was around 50 people who were killed in that hangar, as he said. If we accept these facts, then we can speak of over a hundred people killed in that period. I am not saying, Your Honour, because I didn't see the report, that what he told me is a hundred per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From my side, one concluding question: Could you please discuss what you already intended, the meeting in Pale the 10th of May and the 12th of May, and especially in relation to the 12th of May in detail. Did you go there proprio motu or on invitation? Who participated in the meeting? And yes, I don't want once again to anticipate your answer. Therefore, could you please answer in context about these two meetings in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid there may be a misinterpretation in the transcript, because I spoke of only one meeting, and that was the meeting which I said could have taken place on either the 10th or possibly the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your testimony, page 21 of November 2003 in paragraph 67, you mentioned the following, I quote: "The contact of states, military, and political leadership was evident during the meeting held on 12th May in Pale when I explained the events in Glogova." And just a few minutes ago, you tried to start to explain a meeting held the 10th of May. So was there only one meeting, or were there two meetings? Is that what is reflected in paragraph 67 of your testimony of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't notice this. I had no intention of confusing the issue. Only one meeting was held, and I'm sure it was on the 10th. But I cannot make any connection with the 12th of May. This must have escaped my notice. And therefore, please take into account that in fact in Pale, in Sarajevo, I was there on the 10th, or possibly the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that there was only one meeting, and you were taken by mistake when quoting the 12th of May as the date. But then, please explain. Did you go there spontaneously or had you been invited to come there? And some details of this meeting in Pale, whenever it happened, be it now the 10th or the 11th or the 12th of May. In any event, after the events in Glogova and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I started talking about the way in which I went to that meeting. I think I received an invitation and that somebody told me to go to Pale. They said there was a meeting and that I was required to attend it. I went to Pale together with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please attach names, not refer to "somebody." I think this is such an important event that, no doubt, you will recall who invited you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the municipality, I learned about this, but I really can't remember the name. The best I can do is to say that it could have been the municipal secretary through whom the invitation arrived, or perhaps the SDS office. The secretary in the SDS office was called Ms. Mirjana Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, then. What happened in Pale? In which building was the meeting held and who were the participants in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I arrived at the meeting in Pale, which was already underway. I cannot recall the building with any precision. I assume it was in the Panorama Hotel in Pale. This was my first encounter with Pale because previously when our leadership moved to Pale from Sarajevo, I had not had an opportunity of going up there. The meeting was of the following type: The presidents of the crisis staffs from a large number of municipalities were there. I think there were about 50 participants, presidents of crisis staffs from various municipalities. I had seen most of these people in uniform. It was the practice then for presidents of crisis staffs to wear uniforms. I, however, arrived in civilian clothes. The meeting was chaired, or rather Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Mladic chaired it. When I went in, I concluded that the aim of the meeting was for the presidents of the crisis staffs from various municipalities to report about the security and military situation on the ground. I listened to one or two speakers reporting on their municipalities, and then I asked to be given the floor because I wanted to visit the prime minister and acquaint him with events in Bratunac, and then to return to Bratunac in good time because the journey was quite risky and unsafe since there were many Muslim villages along the road. They accepted my explanation and gave me the floor. I went out in front of a long table behind which there was a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the wall. On that map, the municipalities were coloured in different colours. Parts of municipalities or entire municipalities - I don't remember now - and the practice was for our areas in various municipalities to be marked in blue. I was to show on that match where my municipality was and say what was happening in the municipality as regards military and security issues. I gave my report. I said that we had attacked the village of Glogova. I said that the village had been largely burnt down. I said that I had ordered the attack. Mr. Ratko Mladic listened to me. And of course, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Ostojic did as well. They didn't ask me any questions, but asked me to show exactly where Glogova was. I indicated on the map the location of Glogova and the direction from which we had attacked this village. I don't remember every detail, but this was the first time in my life I had seen Mr. Mladic, and I didn't know what his precise role in all this was, probably because I missed the beginning of the meeting. I know that on the 15th of May, Mr. Mladic was appointed commander of the armed forces of the Republic -- the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and probably this was his first introduction to the people on the ground and the current situation on the ground. I finished my report. And as I said, there was applause in the room after I had given my report. This was a fact which can be confirmed by my driver, whose name is Vidoje Radovic, a policeman from Bratunac who was at the meeting with me. I remember Mr. Ostojic's comment. He said: "Now we can colour Bratunac blue." I explained what this meant. This meant we had taken control of Bratunac and that the Serbs were the force controlling Bratunac. I assumed this also meant that Bratunac had, in fact, acquired the possibility of forming part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After this meeting, I asked to be excused, and I was given permission to leave. I went to see Mr. Dzeric in the government. And for the sake of the truth, I have to say that unlike those who had applauded me, he was very angry. He asked me who had ordered the attack. I said I had, and he was very angry because I had done this. I tried to explain, and I left the government building very worried. And then I went back to Bratunac. This is what I can say about this meeting. If there are any other questions, I am prepared to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no more questions from the side of the Bench. Are there any questions from the side of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have just two brief questions to clarify points that were made by Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let me just take you back to the meeting, the first meeting about which you testified where President Karadzic mentioned the only option left is a Greater Serbia. And you said that was the first time you heard that term. And thereafter you attended a meeting with Zekic, Ostojic, and Mrs. Slobodanka Hrvacanin. Let me ask you, what is the first name of the man named Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic. At that time, he was the deputy president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of your testimony, this meeting that took place in Pale on the 10th or the 11th of May, you mentioned that a Mr. Ostojic said "now we can colour Bratunac blue." Is that the same Ostojic who you mentioned attended the meeting at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. Harmon. It's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes your testimony. And may the witness now please be escorted to his place as accused. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's make use of the remaining time. Let's make use of the five remaining minutes in order to clarify two small, relatively unimportant legal issues. I take it that paragraph 14 of the indictment where it reads "widespread and systematic attack," this paragraph of the indictment supersedes paragraph 5(b) of the plea agreement where it reads "widespread or systematic attack". Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, as you know, it's highly disputed and not yet resolved in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal whether a person can at the same time order and commit a crime. I think it has no impact on the outcome and on the result. Therefore, I would ask the Prosecution, do you see a possibility to withdraw the words "ordered and" and leave it with "committed"? This is just to avoid a lengthy legal debate on the relationship between ordering and committing. I think it's -- this is not the place to discuss this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will give you my answer, if it's appropriate, tomorrow morning or the next time we meet, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any more technical problems to be discussed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I have a number of matters. One is that we have a number of submissions that we will make -- I will tender during the course of my closing remarks in this case. They have been provided to the Registrar, and I assume -- and there is no objection to receipt of these into evidence by the Defence. I understand Your Honour wanted to examine those before concluding whether they are admissible or will be admissible. But I bring that to Your Honours' attention. Then there will be the matter tomorrow, if I am to start first thing with my remarks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fair enough. And I thank you for this that we can check it already now. It saves time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then I will need tomorrow morning quite obviously, the numbering of those exhibits, assuming they are all accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tomorrow as well we should clarify the disparity of the numbering of the statement in November that you have. We seem to be off by one point. I think we have discovered the source of that problem. We can clarify that tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it we all get the correct English version signed by Mr. Deronjic no later than tomorrow in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will leave that to my colleagues from the Defence to deal with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, is in this collection already included a map on the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The map of the area is included as one of our exhibits. It should be the first exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will provide and tender an aerial view of Glogova. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have one minute to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, this is the map, if the usher may... Unfortunately, this is a format which we couldn't -- which we couldn't downsize -- we couldn't downsize that in The Hague. And as you know, we were in rather a rush to get in possession of that document. And we would like to tender it as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. May I ask the Prosecution, are you prepared to present this document? Of course, first we have to see it and you have to see it, in a way that it can be printed? I know about the technical skills of the staff members of the Prosecution, so I have no reasonable doubt that you can manage this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour, for your confidence in our ability to deal with these technical matters. I will certainly explore it with my staff and do everything I can to get it in the right size. By the way, I have seen it, and I have no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then it's -- can we just, Madam Registrar, can we just see it. And this stems from which period of time? Before the attack on Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this image was made in the 1990s, before the attack. This is what the village looked like before the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your assistance. And I hope, with the assistance of the Prosecution, we will get a printable document. Thank you so much to everybody, especially also to the interpreters and everybody who has accompanied us until 7.00. Let's call it a day. And we'll resume tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 7.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of January, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.
